title: Hundreds of migrants swim from Morocco to Spanish enclave of Ceuta
description: Hundreds of migrants have entered Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta from Morocco over the past week, the territory's leader has said.Juan Jesús V
body: Hundreds of migrants have entered Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta from Morocco over the past week, the territory's leader has said.Juan Jesús Vivas said the influx is overwhelming resources and urged the Spanish government to intervene. Spain's Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska is expected to visit on Friday, according to news agency Reuters.Footage showed migrants swimming and using inflatable rings and other flotation devices to swim to Ceuta on Thursday, while others ran through a gate in the border fence.Ceuta, on Morocco's northern coast, is separated from mainland Spain by the Strait of Gibraltar and has long been a focal point for migrants attempting to reach Europe.Earlier this month, the country's Supreme Court ruled that migrants intercepted at sea while trying to reach Ceuta or Melilla cannot be returned to Morocco.Spain's interior ministry said they believed human trafficking networks were exploiting that ruling to "encourage the flow of undocumented migrants, mostly young people".They said they cooperate with Morocco on all areas, including migration, and that both countries have agreed to strengthen efforts to address matter, including "the handover, as soon as possible, of all people who have entered Ceuta illegally".There are conflicting reports on the scale of the crossing, with figures ranging from hundreds to thousands of people.Spanish media estimated between 2,000 and 3,000 people entered Ceuta on Thursday, according to Reuters, but said that the Guardia Civil had not confirmed the figure.Meanwhile, Spain's public broadcaster RTVE reported that "hundreds" crossed into the territory during the day. It also said more than 1,500, mostly young Moroccan migrants, had reached Ceuta over the past two weeks. Vivas said the bodies of 60 people had been recovered at sea in recent months, RTVE reported.He also added the territory was facing a humanitarian and security emergency, warning that reception centres for unaccompanied minors were operating at several times their intended capacity, according to Reuters.The surge has prompted comparisons with May 2021, when around 8,000 people entered Ceuta over a matter of days, exacerbating diplomatic tensions with Morocco.Spain's Ceuta and Melilla enclaves, which are located in North Africa, represent the European Union's only land border with Africa.Spanish authorities have increased security around the enclaves in recent years through increased surveillance, barrier reinforcement, and improved bilateral relations with Morocco, but people continue to attempt to cross.Meanwhile, Italy has called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen zone, with Prime Minister Giorgio Meloni saying they were "prepared to intervene with extraordinary measures to defend the borders and the safety of citizens".In a post on X she said the images from Ceuta were "striking", and show that "uncontrolled illegal immigration poses a concrete threat to the security of Europe's borders".

schema.headline: Hundreds of migrants swim from Morocco to Spanish enclave of Ceuta

title: Prison recalls up 28% in England and Wales, new figures reveal
description: Large rise in offenders sent back to prison, figures revealByTom Edgington and Harriet AgerholmBBC VerifyThere has been a large rise in the number of
body: Large rise in offenders sent back to prison, figures revealByTom Edgington and Harriet AgerholmBBC VerifyThere has been a large rise in the number of offenders being recalled to prisons in England and Wales having been released on licence, new government figures show.There were 51,419 licence recalls in the year ending March 2026, up from 40,259 in the previous year - a 28% increase.Although recalls in January to March were slightly lower than the previous three-month period, they remain well above historical levels.The figures follow government schemes to release a number of offenders early in an effort to ease prison overcrowding.The Ministry of Justice (MOJ) said offenders released on licence face strict conditions "and can be hauled back to prison if they break these rules".Cassia Rowland, from the Institute for Government think tank, said most recalls are for breaches of licence conditions, such as missed appointments, rather than offenders committing further offences or posing a serious risk to the public."The probation service is overwhelmed, with high caseloads and lots of vacancies putting often inexperienced staff under huge pressure," she said.The most common reason provided for prison recalls between January and March was "non-compliance" (9,683), followed by "failed to keep in touch" (5,025).There were 2,891 recalls because an offender faced further charges between January and March 2026, a 23% rise on the same period in 2025. More than one reason can be recorded against each recall.Alex Hewson, from the Prison Reform Trust, said: "Many leave prison facing challenges such as addiction, poor mental health and unstable housing, making compliance with licence conditions difficult."Responding to the figures, the MOJ said "public protection is our priority" and the statistics "show that we do not hesitate to recall offenders to prison when the risk escalates."Sentencing Act release scheme pausedThe increase in prisoner recall comes after the government introduced an early release scheme in England and Wales to help ease overcrowding pressure in September 2024.The scheme meant eligible prisoners could be released after serving 40% of their sentence rather than half.As of March 2026, 70,066 people had been released under the scheme, external.Rowland says early release schemes have contributed to the increase in recalls."But these schemes have also made it harder for prisons and probation to prepare people for release effectively and give them support with basic things like finding accommodation, accessing job support and so on."Despite the releases there were still 86,267 people in England and Wales' prisons, external as of 27 July, meaning the prison estate was 97% full.In a further attempt to ease prison capacity pressure, Sir Keir Starmer's government had planned to release some offenders after serving just one-third of their custodial term.The Sentencing Act release scheme was due to come into force from 2 September, but it has been paused by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham following criticism from survivors and victims' families.The BBC understands around 700 prisoners would have been eligible for early release under the scheme's first phase.Although the prison population has remained relatively stable since 2010, following rapid growth in the 1990s, government projections, external suggest it could rise to about 90,000 in 2028.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Andy Burnham has announced a pause to the Sentencing Act early release schemeUsing early release to manage prison overcrowding is not new.Governments led by Labour and the Conservatives have each introduced emergency measures when the prison system has come under strain.In October 2023, Rishi Sunak's Conservative government began releasing eligible offenders up to 18 days early. The scheme was eventually expanded to up to 70 days ahead of offenders' release date.Nick Hardwick, the former chief inspector of prisons, says early release alone will not solve the problem, arguing "it's just going to slow the rate of growth".New prison plansThe Starmer government announced a plan to add 14,000 new prison places by 2031, external, including four new prisons. It said it would acquire land if necessary and would "make sure the supply always keeps up with demand".The MOJ previously told BBC Verify the government had delivered about 3,200 prison places so far - 1,600 for each of their two years in office. However, this figure only covers new prison places and does not factor in those taken out of use.Hardwick says expanding the number of prisons is only part of the answer because "the one thing you can't do quickly is produce experienced staff."The prison building programme is already costing billions of pounds, he adds, leaving it up to ministers to decide how much they are prepared to spend to keep more people in prison for longer."There's no perfect solution... it's a question of what's the least bad option."Additional reporting by Isobel Cottam

schema.headline: Prison recalls up 28% in England and Wales, new figures reveal

title: Danube's record low levels force shutdown of Hungary's only nuclear plant
description: Image source, EPAImage caption, The level of the water of the Danube is so low that the nuclear power plant's suction nozzles cannot reach itByLaura G
body: Image source, EPAImage caption, The level of the water of the Danube is so low that the nuclear power plant's suction nozzles cannot reach itByLaura Gozzi and Paul KirbyEurope digital editorHungary's only nuclear power plant will be forced to shut down entirely for the first time due to record low water levels of the River Danube, Prime Minister Péter Magyar has said.The Soviet-era Paks power plant uses the Danube for cooling but the water level is so low that the suction nozzles cannot reach it. Magyar warned Hungary's energy supply could become "critical" from Monday due to the Paks shutdown and the ongoing heatwave, which will see temperatures hover around 37C for a week.Like much of Europe, Hungary has seen very low rainfall and high temperatures for much of the summer.The waters of the Danube have fallen to the lowest levels for 30 years in several countries, including neighbouring Serbia and Romania.Magyar asked Hungarians to limit activities that required significant energy consumption between the peak times of 17:00 and 22:00, including charging electric cars and using air conditioning equipment.A "rotational shutdown regime" was also possible if the other combined efforts were not enough to maintain the balance of the national grid, Magyar said, adding the government would compile a list of electricity and water consumers whose consumption could be limited.Image source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, Large areas of the riverbed have been exposed in the centre of Budapest after weeks of extreme heat and droughtIn Romania, one of the country's only two nuclear reactors has been shut down at the Cernavoda power plant, which provides about 20% of the country's power.The first of the two 706-megawatt reactors was shut down earlier this week because the Danube's levels were so low, and state-owned company Nuclearelectrica was trying to avoid closing down the other on Thursday. If the second reactor is shut down Romania will, like Hungary, be temporarily without any nuclear energy production.Climate change is driving up temperatures around the world - but particularly in Europe.It is the fasting warming continent, heating up twice as fast as the global average, according to the Copernicus climate service. This is causing increased summer heatwaves, greater pressure on Europe's waters and more intense wildfires. Image source, ReutersImage caption, Among the wrecks exposed by the low levels of the Danube was a World War Two German warship at Prahovo in SerbiaRomania's National Institute of Hydrology says the average river flow where the Danube enters the country is 4,700 cubic metres per second in July, whereas on Wednesday it was down to less than a third of that, at 1,600cm per second. The institute forecast it would continue to fall to 1,500cm per second by Tuesday.The Danube runs 2,857km (1,775 miles) through 19 countries.The Upper Danube goes from Germany to the Slovak capital Bratislava, the middle basin runs from Bratislava to the border between Serbia and Romania and the Lower Danube extends through Romania and Bulgaria into the three main branches of the Danube Delta that flow into the Black Sea.The low waters of the river have resulted in several unexpected discoveries. The remains of a sunken Hungarian cargo ship resurfaced in Croatia, while the hulks of a German river flotilla was seen in Serbia. And a resident of the northeastern Bulgarian city of Ruse found bones on the Danube river bed, which experts determined were the remains of a mammoth. They were able to recognise a lower jaw, two tusks, and possibly a mammoth rib.Image source, Inquam Photos/Ovidiu Micsik/ReutersImage caption, River flow in Serbia on the Danube is now a third of the average for JulyShipping has ground to a halt on the river in Bulgaria, and border police had to evacuate 186 river cruise passengers from the Viking Ullur ship earlier this week when it ran aground close to Vidin, a city that sits on the border with Romania.  Passengers had been running low on food and water because the cruise ship was unable to dock in Vidin, and another boat that was called in to help was unable to get close enough."I have never heard of such low levels over the years. There has certainly not been a similar situation since 1990," Ivan Zhekov, head of river supervision at Bulgaria's maritime administration agency told BTA news agency.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Boats lie on the dried-out Danube riverbed in front of the Calafat-Vidin bridge, connecting Bulgaria and RomaniaIt is not just the Danube where river levels are low. In Serbia, the levels are also very low on the Sava and Tisa, which are both tributaries of the Danube.Serbian hydrologist Dejan Vladiković said the problems were not just down to the current high temperatures but also to low rainfall during the spring. He told Serbian TV channel N1 that the Danube was down to levels not seen for 50 to 60 years, and climatologists did not expect to see any improvement until mid-September.Temperatures in Serbia are set to climb as high as 38C on Friday, and locally up to 40C, with night-time temperatures in Belgrade as high as 26C.Elsewhere in Europe, forecasters say fire-prone conditions are expected to spread towards central Europe, with Greece and Turkey among the countries worst affected. Vast areas of France and Spain have just experienced some of the most intense and widespread wildfires in living memory, leading to hundreds of thousands of evacuations.

schema.headline: Danube's record low levels force shutdown of Hungary's only nuclear plant

title: Zendaya and Tom Holland: Their decade-long Spider-Man romance in pictures
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Zendaya and Tom Holland first met in 2016ByPaul GlynnCulture reporterNewlyweds Tom Holland and Zendaya steppe
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Zendaya and Tom Holland first met in 2016ByPaul GlynnCulture reporterNewlyweds Tom Holland and Zendaya stepped out together on Wednesday to promote their fourth Spider-Man film together.Over the course of a decade we have seen them grow up together on the big screen.Let's spin a web back to the past and compare how they were when their spider-senses first started tingling together, to now.Spider-Man: Homecoming - 2017Image source, Getty ImagesImage source, Getty ImagesHolland and Zendaya were just 20 and 19 years old, respectively, when they first met in 2016 on the set of Spider-Man: Homecoming, during the movie's casting and initial production.The film showed British actor Holland as Peter Parker balancing high school life with being a superhero - Spider-Man - for the first time.It also introduced US actress Zendaya as Michelle Jones-Watson - aka MJ - his awkward but intellectual classmate.The on-screen chemistry was clear from the start and the film received good reviews but the pair denied rumours of a romance, insisting they were just close friends while promoting the movie.They even took to Twitter [now X] to make light of the rumours. She posted: "Wait wait ... my favourite is when it says we go on vacations together HA! I haven't been on a vacation in years! hbu @TomHolland1996 ???"Holland responded: "Does the press tour count?"Spider-Man: Far From Home - 2019Image source, Getty ImagesImage source, Getty ImagesThe pair continued to film and promote Marvel projects together.They were back on the red carpet together in 2019 for the release of Spider-Man: Far From Home.The movie saw Peter go on a school trip to Europe, where he teamed up with MJ.It also saw them share their first on-screen kiss as their characters grew closer.Spider-Man: No Way Home - 2021Image source, Getty ImagesImage source, Getty ImagesIn summer 2021, the acting pair were photographed embracing in Los Angeles in real life, driving fans online wild.Later that year, they were looking cosy on the campaign trail for Spider-Man: No Way Home, which also saw Zendaya's famous method dressing in her spider-webbed outfit.Their third Spider-Man film together saw multiverse chaos break out after Peter's identity is revealed, with MJ by his side.A few months after the premiere, Holland marked Zendaya's birthday by posting a selfie from the set, alongside the caption: "My MJ, have the happiest of birthdays. Gimme a call when your up xxx."Spider-Man: Brand New Day - 2026Image source, Getty ImagesImage source, Getty ImagesIn recent years, the confirmed couple have been seen together many times at gigs, sports matches and after-parties, but have also both spoken to the media about the need to balance their public and private lives.Speaking to Extra, external on the red carpet at the 2024 Critics' Choice Awards, Holland revealed their favourite collective pastime was rewatching old Spider-Man movies."Zendaya and I will, every now and then, watch Spider-Man 1 and reminisce about being 19 and making those movies again," he said.In June 2026, following years of speculation regarding engagement rings and viral AI wedding pics, Holland, now 30, confirmed they had, in fact, got married.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Zendaya showing her wedding rings at Wednesday's London premiereFigure caption, Zendaya's advice on working with husband Tom HollandSoon after, Hollywood's hottest couple appeared together on the red carpet for Wednesday's London premiere of their fourth Spider-Man story, which picks up years after the events of No Way Home in a world where no-one remembers Peter.On working with her husband, Zendaya, 29, told BBC News: "When you're best friends, it's easy."Tomdaya, as they are affectionately known online, are featuring together in another new film, The Odyssey, but for Spider-Man fans, at least, they will be Peter and MJ forever.Image source, Sony Pictures/MarvelImage caption, The couple appear together on screen again in the latest Spider-Man instalment which is out now in UK cinemasImage source, Sony Pictures/Marvel

schema.headline: Zendaya and Tom Holland: Their decade-long Spider-Man romance in pictures

title: Burnham says he told Trump UK will be pragmatic about North Sea oil
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he told US President Donald Trump he would take a "pragmatic approach" to the issue of North Sea oil and gas.Trum
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he told US President Donald Trump he would take a "pragmatic approach" to the issue of North Sea oil and gas.Trump has long urged the UK to increase drilling and claimed that Burnham had pledged to "open up the North Sea" in their first phone call together. Asked about the president's comments, the new prime minister said: "There is a resource there. When people are struggling - you can't ignore that and hence me indicating that to the president."Burnham has faced pressure from some trade unions, industry figures and some of his own Labour MPs to back increased drilling in the North Sea.In its 2024 general election manifesto, Labour promised not to issue new licences for drilling but said it would honour existing ones.As energy secretary in Sir Keir Starmer's government, Ed Miliband was a staunch supporter of Labour's manifesto position. He has previously described the licence issued to Rosebank, Britain's largest untapped oil and gas field, as "climate vandalism".Miliband is now the foreign secretary in Burnham's government.Although the government has not made any announcements on the issue, Trump has praised what he perceives as a change of stance by the UK government. In a social media post, published the day before Burnham became prime minister,, external Trump wrote: "The People of Aberdeen, in Scotland, are dancing in the streets because the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has stated that he will be opening up, all the way, the invaluable North Sea Oil!"This week, when asked about his conversation with Burnham, Trump said: "He said he's going to open up North Sea oil."If he does that, you're going to be a wealthy country." He later added: "You buy a lot of your energy, as you know, from the North Sea. You buy from Norway and Norway gets it from the North Sea... Norway's got trillions of dollars in the bank." "Scotland has a better part of the North Sea."Asked about Trump's comments, Burnham said: "I indicated in the phone call that we had a week last Monday that I would take a pragmatic approach when it comes to the North Sea, and that is my intention as we go forward from here."In response, Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: "Our country is burning. Crops are failing. Thousands have been killed by extreme heat. "Allowing new oil and gas drilling in the North Sea will worsen the climate breakdown putting more lives at risk and doing untold damage to our economy."It's not too late for Burnham to do the right thing and commit to leaving dangerous fossil fuels in the ground."The Conservatives and Reform have urged the government to approve more drilling in the North Sea, arguing it would reduce energy prices. Last year, Tory Party leader Kemi Badenoch said it would be "absurd" for the UK to leave "vital resources untapped".Some Labour MPs have expressed unease about more drilling, with Rachael Maskell urging the government to "follow the climate science because we have got a climate emergency". Simon Francis, from the End Fuel Poverty Coalition, said: "No household struggling with their energy bills will see a penny come off by drilling more from the North Sea."Gas is sold at the global market prices, so whatever is pumped out is sold to the highest bidder, not handed to British billpayers at a discount."Sir Keir's government had already made concessions, allowing "tie-backs" -  production in unlicensed areas close to or connected to already licensed areas.Currently, the debate over North Sea drilling has focused on two oil and gas fields - Rosebank and Jackdaw, located in Scotland. In 2022 and 2023, regulators approved drilling at the sites, but that was overturned in 2025 following a legal challenge. The legal process is ongoing, but the government will at some point have to decide whether to permit companies to produce oil in the two areas.Other oil and gas licences have been approved in recent years but remain largely undeveloped.If he wanted to encourage more drilling in the North Sea, Burnham could also opt to scrap the Energy Profits Levy, also known as the windfall tax.

schema.headline: Burnham says he told Trump UK will be pragmatic about North Sea oil

title: Four people die after busiest day for small-boat crossings this year
description: Four people died trying to cross the Channel overnight after the busiest day for small-boat crossings so far this year saw 752 arrivals in the UK.One
body: Four people died trying to cross the Channel overnight after the busiest day for small-boat crossings so far this year saw 752 arrivals in the UK.One man died after a vessel capsized off France's northern coast late on Wednesday, local officials said, with a one-year-old child among those hurt.Seven hours later, three people were found dead aboard a small boat after launching from Dunkirk overnight, some 100km (62 miles) up the coast.French officials confirmed their deaths as the Home Office reported that Wednesday saw the highest number of crossings in a single day this year, with nine boats reaching the UK.Local authorities in France said the first boat capsized off the coast at Hardelot around 23:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday.The man is thought to have been in his 30s or 40s, officials added. Six other people including the child sustained minor injuries.Local officials said the vessel was a "taxi" boat - which cruise along the coast and pick up their paying customers who are waiting in the sea.Security officials "neutralised" the boat and an investigation into the incident has been launched.The second boat launched from the Dunkirk area overnight was spotted near a breakwater off the coast at 06:00, the French coastguard said.Search and rescue officials subsequently found three unconscious people aboard. Their deaths were later confirmed by emergency medical personnel.A UK government spokesperson said: "Every death in the Channel is a tragedy and a stark reminder of the dangers posed by criminal gangs exploiting vulnerable people for profit."Prime Minister Andy Burnham, speaking separately about small boat crossings on Thursday, said the UK had made "significant progress" on reducing the number of arrivals.But, asked by reporters about US President Donald Trump's remark that the UK had a "huge immigration problem", Burnham said there was much still to do "to get those numbers right down".Conservative shadow home secretary Chris Philp called the deaths "preventable" and said the only way to save lives was "to stop the crossings completely".He said a "proper deterrent" was required, adding: "If they [migrants] know they will be quickly removed, then they will not cross in the first place."The Refugee Council said the deaths were "heartbreaking" and stressed that "those who risk dangerous small boat journeys do so only out of desperation"."Fewer refugees would risk Channel crossings if the government created safe pathways for people to come to the UK, like they previously did for people coming from Ukraine, Syria and Afghanistan," said its external affairs director Imran Hussain.A total of 162 people died in the English Channel between 2018 and 2025, according to the University of Oxford's Migration Observatory.Small-boat crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020.Wednesday's 752 arrivals surpassed the year's previous daily high of 710 recorded in June, and brings the provisional total for the year to 14,128 - which is 42% lower than the number recorded by this time last year.The Home Office has said this is not just down to weather conditions but also its work with French authorities to prevent crossings by ensuring enforcement action on beaches and seizing boats, including a £662m deal signed in April.Wednesday's figure is the highest number recorded in one day since 20 December 2025, when there were 803 arrivals - but is well below the 1,305 arrivals recorded on 3 September 2022.Last week, a record 165 migrants arrived in a single boat.Additional reporting by Dan Wainwright, BBC Verify

schema.headline: Four people die after busiest day for small-boat crossings this year

title: Alan Shearer: Challenging times ahead for Newcastle after Eddie Howe exit
description: Thank you, Eddie Howe. You gave me the best day of my life as a Newcastle fan.Whatever the reasons are for him leaving the club, I think every support
body: Thank you, Eddie Howe. You gave me the best day of my life as a Newcastle fan.Whatever the reasons are for him leaving the club, I think every supporter of my age or younger - and I am 55 - would say the same.Eddie will always be a legend in the eyes of the Geordie public for ending our long wait for a major trophy with that epic day he gave us at Wembley when we won the Carabao Cup in 2025.I had craved that moment for my entire life. I had been to Wembley before as a Toon player and I had been there before as a Toon fan, and we'd all had the same feeling of walking away empty-handed.He will be remembered for changing that, and we have to say a massive thank you for everything else he has done since he took charge in November 2021, when the club were 19th in the Premier League, five points adrift of safety after 11 games.Eddie kept us up that year, then finished fourth, seventh and fifth in the next three seasons, with some amazing nights in the Champions League along the way. He did a brilliant job.The best way of showing how far we have come under him is that we finished 12th last season and it was a disappointment, but I would not blame him for that, either.What happened last summer massively hindered Newcastle, with Alexander Isak leaving and the club missing out on their main transfer targets.Unfortunately, that trend has continued this year. I would not be surprised if it influenced Eddie's thinking about whether to stay or go, and it also makes me worry about what will happen next.Speaking purely as a fan, I think we have to get ready for a tough season and some very challenging times ahead.The timing of Eddie's exit is the biggest surprise for me - three weeks into pre-season, and with only three weeks to go until the Premier League starts again.I don't know exactly what has gone on behind the scenes for this to happen now but I guess, from his point of view, he was seeing his best players being sold - first Isak, then Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali this summer - and with speculation over captain Bruno Guimaraes' future too.He has probably thought it was a tough enough job anyway, but it is just getting tougher.You cannot keep on selling your best players and then hope to be in contention at the top of the table - I hope I'm wrong but it is probably inevitable that Bruno will be next to leave.Whatever Bruno's intentions were before, when Eddie was in charge, then he must look now and think well, we are selling our stars and now the manager, who he clearly had a great rapport with, has gone too.It's not just the players leaving that is a bad look, it is seeing a series of attempted signings fail to get over the line as well.Hugo Ekitike, Johan Manzambi and Victor Munoz all went to Liverpool or Aston Villa ahead of Newcastle in the past 12 months and now it also looks like James Trafford has chosen Leeds instead.That's something else that Eddie has maybe looked at, because there has to be a reason why Newcastle are not getting so many of their targets.Losing the manager on top of all this is a huge blow, especially a high-calibre one like Eddie who is going to get some huge job offers from home and abroad off the back of his achievements at St James' Park.I think even someone really experienced would find the situation a difficult one and Matthias Jaissle, who is expected to get the job, is only 38.While he has been successful with Al-Ahli in Saudi Arabia, you cannot really compare that to working in the Premier League, which is a completely different beast.Take a step back and, whether we like it or not, we can all see what is happening with all the ins and outs at Newcastle. Whatever statements come out of the club, it is clear the landscape has changed.It is a changing football club - in terms of its owners' aims and ambitions and their transfer strategy, which all seem massively different to the way they were even three years ago.Back then the sky seemed to be the limit, and the talk was about competing with the very best.Now, the approach seems to be to sell their best players and replace them with younger, hungry and up-and-coming prospects. If it was that easy to do it successfully and still compete at the top of the table, then everyone would do it - but it isn't.The club's spending always had to comply with the Premier League's profitability and sustainability rules but it still felt like the plan was to battle it out for silverware every season.Go back to the summer of 2023, when Newcastle had just finished fourth and added Tonali, Harvey Barnes and Tino Livramento to a squad already containing Isak, Gordon and Bruno.It felt like they were ready to challenge for everything, and capable of beating everyone. Howe had made them a horrible team to play against, in the nicest possible way.Three years on, much of that team has gone and now the manager has too, but it is the whole model which feels the most different.The goalposts have moved massively from where the club said they wanted to get to, compared to where they are now.When we won the Carabao Cup, I was hoping it was just the start of something very special, but it seems a lot has changed since then.Alan Shearer was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

schema.headline: Alan Shearer: Challenging times ahead for Newcastle after Eddie Howe exit

title: Archbishop of Canterbury committed to £100m slavery fund
description: This is Dame Sarah's first pastoral visit to Africa since being installed as head of the Church of England at a ceremony in Canterbury Cathedral in Ma
body: This is Dame Sarah's first pastoral visit to Africa since being installed as head of the Church of England at a ceremony in Canterbury Cathedral in March.Reparative justice has been one of the themes running through the Ghana leg of this trip.At Cape Coast Castle, which came under British control in the 1660s, Dame Sarah was shown dungeons where slaves were held, and the so-called "door of no return" through which they were forced on to ships.The archbishop said: "You can't help but be deeply moved by the horrific conditions that people were kept in and the way that they were treated."It completely throws you off balance and brings home the evil that was transatlantic slavery."Above the dungeons sits a chapel, which she said was a "stark illustration of the way the church was involved in the slave trade".The Church of England has previously apologised for its associations with the slave trade.Its missionary arm ran slave-farmed plantations in the Caribbean to fund the spread of Anglicanism, individual members of clergy were slave owners, and the Church received large donations from slave traders.

schema.headline: Archbishop of Canterbury committed to £100m slavery fund

title: Diane Abbott readmitted into Labour Party after suspension
description: Image source, Jeff Overs/ BBCUpdated 3 minutes agoThe long-serving MP Diane Abbott has been let back into the Labour Party, following a year-long susp
body: Image source, Jeff Overs/ BBCUpdated 3 minutes agoThe long-serving MP Diane Abbott has been let back into the Labour Party, following a year-long suspension.In a statement, a Labour spokesperson said Abbott had "apologised" following an independent process and that she would be readmitted into the parliamentary party, meaning she can sit as a Labour MP once again.Abbott, who was suspended in 2025 following an antisemitism row, said she had been "issued with a formal warning". East Kilbride and Strathaven MP Joani Reid has also been readmitted to the party. In March, she said she had "voluntarily" suspended herself after her husband was arrested on suspicion of spying for China.Her husband David Taylor, was arrested along with two other men. All three have been released on police bail, which in May was extended until August.Responding to her readmittance on Thursday evening, Reid she was "excited to play a full part in supporting our new prime minister".She added: "I have never been part of a police investigation, as a suspect or as a witness, and I am pleased that this has now been recognised."A Labour spokesperson said the decisions about party membership had been taken "independently of the leadership and political interference".Abbott, the MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington, was initially suspended in 2023 over a letter to the Observer newspaper, external in which she said Irish, Jewish and Traveller people "undoubtedly experience prejudice" but "they are not all their lives subject to racism". She was readmitted to Labour shortly before the 2024 general election however, in a BBC interview just over a year ago she said she did not regret the incident and defended her original remarks. This led to her second suspension in July 2025 and since then she has been sitting as an independent MP.In a post on X,, external Abbott wrote: "Today, following a process conducted in line with party rules and approved by the independent review process I have been readmitted to the Labour party."She said she had been "issued with a formal warning for a tweet I previously posted", in which she referred to the Israel Defense Forces as the 'Jewish Defence Force'."I used wording that conflates the actions of the state of Israel with the Jewish community. I am deeply sorry for any hurt caused by that conflation and apologise for any hurt caused by it."She added: "I have been and remain a lifelong anti-racist and remain deeply committed to opposing racism in all of its forms."The post about the Israel Defense Forces was posted days before her suspension in July 2025.Image source, PA MediaSome Labour MPs had been calling for Abbott to be readmitted to Labour and more than 38,000 people had signed a petition backing her return. Earlier, following reports in the Sun newspaper, external about Abbott's possible readmission, Jewish groups expressed concern.The Board of Deputies said: "This is an early test of resolve for the Burnham administration."It is hard to conceive of the whip being restored unless there is clear and sustained evidence of genuine remorse, a proper understanding of why those comments were so hurtful, and an unequivocal recognition that antisemitism is racism."While people can learn from their mistakes, Diane Abbott's past record is not encouraging in this regard."The Jewish Leadership Council said the prime minister "must explain how returning that whip to Diane Abbott is consistent with this zero tolerance approach to antisemitism."Following the party's decision to accept Abbott and Reid back into the parliamentary party, two MPs remain suspended from Labour.Karl Turner was suspended in March for making "uncollegiate" comments about colleagues, BBC News understands. However, Turner said it was "clear" his suspension was due to his criticism of the government's policy on jury trials. Dan Norris, the MP for North East Somerset and Hanham, was suspended after being arrested on suspicion of sexual offences.

schema.headline: Diane Abbott readmitted into Labour Party after suspension

title: Greens review social media operation as Polanski row rumbles on
description: The Green Party of England and Wales is reviewing its social media operation which has been central to its surge in popularity over the past year, sou
body: The Green Party of England and Wales is reviewing its social media operation which has been central to its surge in popularity over the past year, sources have told the BBC.They insist it is not connected to the backlash to Zack Polanski this week after he re-posted a photo of a man wearing a t-shirt with an image of a guillotine and the slogan "we're only making plans for Nigel" - seen as being a reference to Nigel Farage.But that incident has raised questions about whether it is sustainable for the Green Party leader to manage his own social media channels, with one party figure calling it an "avoidable mistake" and that Polanski "should have said sorry" for it.In an interview with BBC Newsnight, Polanski repeatedly refused to apologise for "an inadvertent mistake" but acknowledged he needed to "be better on social media"."I just didn't look carefully enough and I accepted it, as soon as I was aware of what happened I unaccepted it and took it down," he said.Like other high profile figures on social media, Polanski receives a lot of material from other users seeking re-posts. But unlike most political leaders in the UK, he still manages his own accounts, rather than handing control to party staffers.This may allow him to appear spontaneous and authentic - both valuable commodities on social media - but it comes with risks. The current row began after Polanski shared a single post on Instagram that contained a carousel of 20 pictures.The re-post was shared to Polanski's 713,000 followers, because he accepted a request to tag him as a collaborator, which on the platform makes him a "co-author," placing it on his page and into his followers' feeds.Polanski said he had not noticed the offending image among the others on the post.According to him, he had accepted collaborator tags for eight other posts from the same event in Bristol alone.Reform UK leader Farage claimed the t-shirt amounted to incitement to murder and his party reported it to the police. Neither the Metropolitan Police nor Avon and Somerset Police say the incident meets the threshold for further action.But the political row has continued with Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick calling Polanski a "nasty piece of work", at a news conference earlier on Thursday.Inside the Green Party, there has been some criticism of Polanski's behaviour online.He has attracted positive and negative attention for the rate at which he posts, comments, likes and replies across multiple platforms including X, Bluesky, Facebook and Instagram.And this is not the first time a quick reaction has attracted controversy; last month he had to apologise to police after posting about their response to the Golders Green attack. One senior party source said it was clear that due diligence had not been done on Polanski's social media output, and that moving forwards he needs "tight controls" to stay credible, while keeping a similar tone of engagement with his followers.They pointed out that the speed and number of Polanski's interactions came with a "small upside" but a "colossal downside", and with the latest incident he had "shot himself in the foot at precisely the wrong time".It comes as recent polling suggests the Green Party has lost ground to Labour, following Andy Burnham's election as Labour leader, and down from a peak earlier this year.They added their concerns about a wider problem with the party's vetting on social media and of candidates, including around antisemitic posts in recent months.Several candidates in recent elections have stood down over their social media activity, with two candidates arrested during May's local elections, and another suspended after being elected.But Green Party peer and former deputy mayor of London Baroness Jones said the criticism of Polanski's Instagram re-post seemed to be "mainly from our opponents, not internal discussions".She said that her party leader had "made a mistake", adding "we've all done it and got flak."But she added: "His online presence is what makes him relatable".Along with relatability, comes popularity: Polanski is the second-most followed UK leader on Instagram after Nigel Farage. The Greens surpassed other parties to become the most popular on the platform this year.It is also seen as where a good portion of their voters spend time, as they are the most popular party among the under-30s, according to pollsters YouGov.A separate party source confirmed there was a review going on internally into the party's social media operation, but would not be drawn on whether that meant changing who had oversight of Polanski's posts."We are looking at our processes and systems in this area," they said."Obviously Zack is really active on social media. It is how we have grown our reach and our membership."Until around a year ago the party's entire social media team consisted of one full-time employee.That has now gone up to three or four and may increase further following the review. "We have expanded hugely as a party and we are looking at how we work," the source said."As part of that we are looking at what we might do to support and beef up our social media team."They said the coverage of the Instagram re-post row had been "deeply irritating" but added that the review was not directly linked to that incident.But it remains to be seen how much longer Polanski can retain control of his accounts before handing over the passwords to party staffers.

schema.headline: Greens review social media operation as Polanski row rumbles on

title: Drought declared for whole of Wales amid sustained high temperatures
description: Drought declared across whole of Wales as conditions 'deteriorate'Image source, EPABySteffan MessengerWales environment correspondent and Oliver SlowB
body: Drought declared across whole of Wales as conditions 'deteriorate'Image source, EPABySteffan MessengerWales environment correspondent and Oliver SlowBBC WalesA drought has been extended across the whole of Wales with the country on course for its driest July on record in 190 years.Declaring the drought, the country's environment body Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said sustained high temperatures were causing the condition of the natural environment to "deteriorate".The decision has been made in response to record-low river levels, dry soils, widespread wildfires and mounting impacts on wildlife, farming and forestry.NRW had already announced a drought across the north and parts of mid Wales last week.Image source, Tudur DaviesImage caption, The lack of rain in Wales has led to low water levels in reservoirs like Llyn Aled Isaf in Conwy last weekThe nationwide announcement made on Thursday will trigger more monitoring of rivers and stronger advice for the public on use of water.The declaration of a drought does not mean there is currently a threat to water supplies for homes and businesses, with Welsh water companies saying reservoir levels are holding up after a wet start to the year.NRW said figures had shown Wales had received 8% of its long-term average rainfall for July, with most rivers in the country "exceptionally low".Groundwater levels are also falling in Wales, with some lower than expected for the time of year.The environmental body said its teams were dealing with reports of "wide-reaching impacts to the environment", and that "conditions across Wales' natural environment have continued to deteriorate".This includes drying riverbeds, fish in distress, an accumulation of algae, wildfire risk and concern from farmers about crop growth, grazing conditions and water availability for livestock.Image source, BBC Weather Watchers / NadzenaImage caption, Parched land has been seen across much of Wales this week, including in this park in Dinas Powys, Vale of GlamorganRhian Thomas, from NRW, said the toll from the recent dry weather had been "clear to see", and teams were closely monitoring forecasts and river flows."With no strong indications for notable rainfall in the forecasts, and risks of further heatwaves over the summer, it's more important than ever that we all use water wisely," she said."Every drop we waste is less water for our rivers and wildlife when they need it the most."The dry weather in recent weeks has also coincided with a number of wildfires across Wales.A fire that broke out earlier this month in the Rhinogydd mountains in Gwynedd could be seen from space, with a firefighting helicopter deployed to tackle the blaze.Residents were evacuated from their homes following a fire close to Conwy Mountain said they had heard the blaze, which had sounded "like popcorn", coming down the mountain.First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said he had organised a summit to look at the risks of fires from severe droughts.Speaking to Matt Chorley on BBC Radio 5 Live, he said while there was no "immediate risk to the provision of drinking water", there needed to be "more resilience in our water supplies" across Wales and the UK.Image caption, George Tomlinson says the dry weather makes him worry about the future of farmingGeorge Tomlinson, 29, who runs Rossett Park Farming in Wrexham, said he had to sell 60 cows because the drought had killed off grazing land."There's nothing available for the cows to eat on the grazing platform apart from a little bit of dead grass some dry cows are eating," said Tomlinson, adding "you've got to make tough decisions in order to survive".He said he was also worried about what the future might hold with warmer summers expected."If this continues a lot of farmers will be forced to close their gates and never open them again," he said, describing it as "depressing". Image caption, Farmer Richard Anthony says his land is as hard as a "rock" and has "no moisture at all"Richard Anthony, whose farm stretches over the Vale of Glamorgan and Bridgend county, said the ground on his land was as hard as a "rock" and had "no moisture at all".The dry land has left Anthony unable to plant his crops, who added he had "never ever been in this situation" before."As soon as we've harvested the one crop, we plant in the next crop, but we can't do any of that now," he said. "I've never seen it as bad as this."Our wheat deals are down between 20% and 30%. That is massive. we'll have to cope, we will survive, but the knock-on effect is huge."Anthony said he is concerned that once the rain comes it will not  stop, leaving him unable to plant next year's crops."It'll go from this to being too wet", he added.National Farmers Union Cymru president Abi Reader has warned that the cost of the continuing dry and hot weather will have a financial impact on farmers."We're going to see costs for these farms rising, because they might be having to buy in extra feed for their livestock, or they might be spending a lot of money carting water," she said."We've been in this a long time now, and it's going to take a long time to recover, and absolutely everybody needs to remember that food security starts with water security," she added.What is a drought?A drought occurs when a prolonged lack of rainfall and high temperatures causes severe stress to natural ecosystems.NRW says it results in critically low river and groundwater levels as well as dry soils - which has an impact on wildlife, fisheries and protected habitats.It also has impacts for farming and forestry - such as failing crops - while private water supplies like natural springs and boreholes can run dry.A declaration of environmental drought triggers more monitoring of rivers and releases from reservoirs to help top up the flow.Those who have licences to take water from rivers - from farms and canals to golf courses - will face restrictions.There's a big communications element to this too - so it means firmer advice for the public on using water wisely.There is a difference between NRW's drought announcements and those made by water companies.Welsh Water already have a hosepipe ban in place for parts of west Wales as a result of unprecedented demand during the recent heatwaves, making it harder to process and deliver enough water around the network.But they say there is currently no threat to drinking water supplies and reservoir levels are holding up.

schema.headline: Drought declared for whole of Wales amid sustained high temperatures

title: Palestine Action ban to be reviewed by Supreme Court
description: The controversial ban under terrorism legislation of the protest group Palestine Action will be reviewed by the Supreme Court.In a major blow to the H
body: The controversial ban under terrorism legislation of the protest group Palestine Action will be reviewed by the Supreme Court.In a major blow to the Home Office, the court confirmed on Thursday that it had given the group's co-founder permission to appeal the ban which came into effect in July 2025.While the full details of the reasons for the appeal are yet to be published, the BBC understands they relate to Huda Ammori's argument that the ban breaches human rights.Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said in a statement the government would "robustly defend this appeal".Officials at the court say the appeal will be expedited - which means it will be heard after the summer break. The eventual outcome of the case could have major implications for terrorism legislation in the UK.The decision comes weeks after the end of the first major trial of members of the group which had caused more than £1m of damage to a defence firm near Bristol with an Israeli parent company. Four members of that break-in team were jailed, with one also sentenced for causing grievous bodily harm on a police officer who was hit with a sledgehammer.Separately, more than 2,000 people are facing potential trial for protesting against the ban by declaring their support for a proscribed terrorism group in mass demonstrations.The battle over the banning of Palestine Action has now gone on for more than year. Former Home Secretary Yvette Cooper banned the group on advice from the police and security officials after an escalating spate of break-ins targeting Elbit, an Israeli-owned defence firm.The High Court initially ruled that the ban was unlawful - but five judges on the Court of Appeal then overruled it, unanimously deciding the  home secretary had acted lawfully and within her powers to proscribe Palestine Action.That decision by the Court of Appeal will now be reviewed by the Supreme Court.During Thursday, some 117 protesters were arrested outside Westminster Magistrates' Court, with the Metropolitan Police saying the majority of arrests were for expressing support for the group.Scores of protesters had turned up there because they had expected to appear in court accused of allegedly showing support for the group at earlier public events. However, those cases had been listed in error. Many of the defendants said that they felt they had no choice but to turn up, despite the court and Metropolitan Police telling them not to do so. Palestine Action co-founder Ammori welcomed the Supreme Court's decision to hear her appeal - and said that the latest arrests were part of a wider crackdown on Palestinian solidarity."We will continue to fight this proscription all the way to the Supreme Court and, if necessary, to the European Court of Human Rights to overturn what has become one of the most extreme attacks on free speech and the right to protest in modern British history."The Home Office has repeatedly said that the ban of the group has nothing to do with protest in support of Palestinian causes - and was necessary because it was causing significant criminal damage to legitimate businesses.Both the High Court and the Court of Appeal have ruled that Palestine Action's activities include criminal acts - although they were divided on whether those incidents justified turning to terrorism laws.Those laws - approved by MPs in Parliament - allow the government to ban a group for either serious violence or serious criminal damage for an ideological cause - and trigger wider powers for the police to investigate and charge suspects for organising activities and fundraising.Mahmood said: "The Court of Appeal's judgment upholds the proscription of Palestine Action and we will robustly defend this appeal at the UK Supreme Court."The court has found that Palestine Action has carried out acts of terrorism, celebrated those who have taken part in those acts and promoted the use of violence. It is not an ordinary protest or civil disobedience group, and its actions are not consistent with democratic values and the rule of law."This decision does not affect lawful protest in support of the Palestinian cause, which remains a fundamental democratic right. There is a difference between supporting Palestine and supporting a proscribed terrorist group."We will always take the strongest possible action to protect our national security and keep the public safe."

schema.headline: Palestine Action ban to be reviewed by Supreme Court

title: Why do parts of England and Wales keep falling into drought?
description: More than half of England and the whole of Wales has been declared to be in drought this week - the third such event over the past five years.Farmers
body: More than half of England and the whole of Wales has been declared to be in drought this week - the third such event over the past five years.Farmers have described suffering from reduced yields and being forced to harvest earlier, and field fires increasing.The drought comes despite winter bringing above average rainfall, and reservoirs still close to expected levels for this time of year.So why are parts of the country struggling to get hold of water?There is no single definition of drought, according to the Environment Agency (EA), it depends on who is impacted, the availability of water and its use.A drought can affect things including the environment, farming, or the water supply - what response the government and industry take depends on what the drought is affecting.Possible measures include rescuing and relocating fish, increased business checks on water usage, and redistribution of water supplies. Image gallerySkip image galleryImage source, Suffolk Fire and Rescue ServiceImage caption, A firefighter talks a huge blaze on Dunwich Heath, Suffolk which has caused thousands to be evacuated from their homesSlide 1 of 5, Firefighter sprays liquid at fire through yellow hose. The fire burns heathland in front of them, with smoke rising in to the air, A firefighter talks a huge blaze on Dunwich Heath, Suffolk which has caused thousands to be evacuated from their homesBut currently, nearly all water companies are at drought level 1 - Anglian is the exception at 2 - out of a possible maximum of 4.It is rivers and groundwater levels which have been significantly impacted by a sudden drop in rainfall.South East England relies more heavily on groundwater - where rainfall is stored beneath the surface in pore spaces and fractures in the rock. Chalk areas across the country - from the Yorkshire Wolds to the Wessex Downs - are all reporting levels either at expected or below normal for this time of year, with the Cotswolds particularly struggling.But these groundwater stores "respond more slowly to changes in the climate than rivers, which is why they provide a useful buffer during periods of drought", said Prof Alan MacDonald of the British Geological Survey.Wales has received just 8% of its average rainfall so far this month. England has received 7% of its average, with that figure as low as 1% across southern England. Therefore, groundwater levels are expected to drop even further still.The low rainfall and high temperatures, which increase evaporation rates, have hit rivers hardest. The EA said nearly 80% of England's rivers are seeing flows below normal or lower - the River Thames at Reading has recorded its lowest level on record.Farmers source water for their crops and livestock over summer from a combination of stored winter rainfall on site, and by extracting it from natural sources - a process called abstraction.This can be from groundwater or from surface water, like rivers and streams. So, as levels drop, this becomes a serious issue.Eleanor Gilbert told Radio 4's Today programme that the hot weather has been "very tough" on her farm in Berkshire, which has recorded "less than 30mm of rain since the end of March".Moisture content has to be at a specific level for harvesting different crops.Gilbert said they have been harvesting at 03:00 BST to bring the moisture up, as at that time of day it's cooler and water condenses.But the dry conditions caused by the hot weather have prevented the grain from swelling. It means the farm's yield is down to almost half of what it was the previous year.The EA and Natural Resource Wales grant abstraction licences to farms, but when water levels drop they can impose what is called a "hands-off flow restriction". This means farms are prevented from abstracting water, this is to protect the environment. There are currently 1,353 of these restrictions in place. The EA has also warned that voluntary restrictions may be put in place next month - when farmers are asked to reduce their volumes of water use, only irrigate at night or on certain days of the week. Ben Andrews, a mixed organic farmer in north Herefordshire, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he has had an abstraction licence restriction since the start of the month. "We will have paid for the plants, paid for the labour, if we don't get to pick any of them then it's investment that's lost."Even with these measures in place there have been 61 environmental incidents due to the drought, such as reported fish deaths which, although lower than last year, are rapidly increasing and thought to be underestimated. , externalClimate change is raising global temperatures, which in the UK is expected to lead to drier summers and more intense and longer lasting heatwaves - both of which could contribute to lower river and groundwater levels.On Wednesday, the National Drought Group - which includes regulators, the government, the Met Office, water companies, farmers, the Canal & River Trust, anglers and conservation experts - held a briefing with Water Minister Emma Hardy.The Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said the group reviewed the impact of the drought in England, the country's preparedness and response to it.Hardy said: "We're delivering long-term change in the water industry and driving record investments in infrastructure, including nine new reservoirs."We expect water companies to follow their drought plans, to go further and faster to reduce leaks, and to ensure supplies are not disrupted even in the driest of weather.""We need to invest for the long term, in new water storage facilities, whether it's at the local level supporting farmers or at a large scale with the water companies themselves being allowed to build reservoirs," Sir John Armitt, former chairman of the National Infrastructure Commission, told Radio 4's Today programme on Thursday. He said for a long time governments have resisted building new reservoirs on the basis other solutions could be found, but the recent weather extremes the UK has been experiencing "have really caught people out".There has been no major reservoir completed in England since 1992. Sir Jon Cunliffe, former Bank of England deputy governor, reviewed the sector last year and concluded that there had been "underinvestment" - blaming both the water industry and regulators. Sir John Armitt also said that the industry must also tackle leakage and usage. "That's beholden on all of us to try to reduce the amount we use, and we could save a similar amount if we could get down to the levels of Denmark who use about 100 litres per person a day." The average use per person in the UK is around 140 litres.Water UK, which represents the industry, said at the time, in response: "Everyone agrees the system has not been working.... fundamental change has been long overdue."There are currently two reservoirs pencilled for completion in 2036 and the 2040s, and more set to be approved.In May last year, the government said that water companies had committed to bringing nine new reservoirs by 2050.They would be located in Lincolnshire, Cambridgeshire, Oxfordshire, Somerset, Suffolk, Kent, East Sussex, and the West Midlands.The government said that these reservoirs have the potential to provide 670 million litres of extra water per day.Additional reporting by Tom Ingham, Charlotte Hadfield and Ella Kipling.

schema.headline: Why do parts of England and Wales keep falling into drought?

title: Joe Root: England Test captaincy could be exactly what batter needs, says Michael Vaughan
description: Former skipper Michael Vaughan has said the England Test captaincy could be "exactly what Joe Root needs".Speaking on the Test Match Special podcast,
body: Former skipper Michael Vaughan has said the England Test captaincy could be "exactly what Joe Root needs".Speaking on the Test Match Special podcast, Vaughan said the 35-year-old's return to the role, having led the team from 2017 to 2022, might prove to be motivation in the later stages of his career."I just wonder from Joe's perspective if he needed this to get that real enthusiasm to get up every morning to play Test match cricket," said Vaughan."The amount of cricket that he's played, I just wonder whether he needed this little trigger, this little motivational tool."He hasn't got that many of his close friends in the team any more, a lot of his team-mates have retired or moved on, so maybe this is exactly what Joe Root needs as well."Root returns to the captaincy under the charge of interim head coach Marcus Trescothick after Brendon McCullum was sacked, before New Zealander Stephen Fleming takes over the Test leadership for this winter's tour of South Africa.He stepped down as captain in 2022 after a 10-wicket loss to West Indies, their ninth match without a win, citing the "toll" and "impact" the role had on him.However, Vaughan stated he believed Root had been dealt a "dodgy hand" during his time as Test captain."Around the time he was appointed England were trying to win the 50-over World Cup and all the England eggs were put in the white-ball basket," said Vaughan."Then Covid struck. None of us would know how hard it would be to captain in a Covid time - Joe had to do that. "That Caribbean tour where it came to an end, it looked like a job that was a little bit too far for him. He's a little bit older, a little bit wiser. I think Stephen Fleming will help out with a lot of the stuff that some captains get drained by - organising the dressing room and making sure the tactical side of the team is in good order."I just think in terms of his motivation and in terms of what is left for Joe Root to achieve in the game, of course there's a few runs to get past Sachin [Tendulkar's all-time Test run-scoring record] but if he can be an Ashes winner next year, a world leader in runs he's scored in Test cricket, you can't ask for a more perfect career."Fleming has been appointed on a four-year deal that will mean he coaches England in the next two Ashes series, and Vaughan said managing director Rob Key has selected a "very experienced" option.Former England Test coach Andy Flower was initially linked with the role, but Royal Challengers Bengaluru and London Spirit coach ruled himself out of the process.Fleming joins after leaving Chennai Super Kings this month, having coached the Indian Premier League (IPL) franchise for the past nine seasons."Andy Flower, I think from what I've read is the one that they wanted. He turned that down so it was like 'OK, how do we get the next best?'" Vaughan said of Fleming."Some will say he's not coached in red-ball cricket but you've got a very experienced manager, very experienced coach who's been around the modern game with Chennai Super Kings over the course of the last few years. "He was a very, very good captain back in the day, a very good tactician, renowned for being a really good man-manager. "Having McCullum still as the white-ball coach and then having someone coaching the Test team who doesn't know McCullum, that could have been really tricky. "I think Stephen Fleming has been brought in for that reason - he's obviously very close to McCullum. "They needed someone who could work with McCullum because someone that doesn't know Baz and his style, I think it could have got very, very messy."Fleming, who retired from playing in 2009, has a wealth of experience in Test cricket, making 111 appearances for New Zealand, scoring 7,172 runs with an average of 40.06 in the middle order.McCullum was known for promoting an aggressive form of cricket, dubbed Bazball by fans and the media, but Vaughan said Fleming will have to make changes to England's style and technique."I'm kind of sick and tired of talking about England's style of play. The style of play I want to see is England winning," Vaughan added. "Whatever that style is on that given day, session, hour, England have to play the right style of cricket that wins games of cricket. "We can only talk about talent and the gulf of talent in English cricket for so long - they've got to start winning games of cricket and winning trophies now."The one thing this Test team needs is coaching the technical side of batting. "How many of them can look themselves in the mirror and when Michael Neser, Matt Henry, Scott Boland bowls that good length just on or around that off stump, can play a controlled forward defence shot? "They won't like saying it and they won't like talking about technique, but technique wins Test match cricket and the technical side of England's players and batting has been found wanting. "So it's all right putting a good leader of the group, but I also think they need one or two changes in the backroom team to make sure these players are getting really well coached as well."

schema.headline: Joe Root: England Test captaincy could be exactly what batter needs, says Michael Vaughan

title: US launches 'heavy' strikes on Iran after attempted attack on American troops
description: The US military says it has completed a "heavy wave" of strikes against Iran in retaliation for Tuesday's attempted ballistic missile attacks on Ameri
body: The US military says it has completed a "heavy wave" of strikes against Iran in retaliation for Tuesday's attempted ballistic missile attacks on American forces.Centcom said it hit "dozens" of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in response to Iran's firing on US bases in Jordan and at ships in the Strait of Hormuz.Iranian state media said the latest strikes had killed three people, including a two-year-old child, on Qeshm island, while other locations were also hit in the south and west of the country.The latest hostilities come on a week that has seen the conflict expand, with the first publicly announced joint US-Saudi strikes targeting Iranian proxies in Iraq.Iran and the US have engaged in escalating strikes and counter-strikes since a ceasefire in April, aimed at pausing the months-long war, fell apart in June. The US has blockaded Iranian ports and bombed Iranian sites, while Iran has fired missiles and drones at US assets in countries across the Middle East and targeted shipping in the economically important Strait of Hormuz, connecting the Gulf and Arabian Sea.On Wednesday, news outlet Axios cited an unnamed US official as saying that Trump had met Saudi defence minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, who had conveyed that Saudi Arabia wants to de-escalate tensions. The BBC has contacted the White House for comment. Analysis: Saudi Arabia's dilemma as it tries to stay out of US-Iran warMeanwhile, the Egyptian government said a fire at a port on Wednesday had been caused by a drone attack. Egypt, a US ally, has not previously been directly attacked during the war.The US-Iran conflict has reignited after several days of relative calm.For days, both sides halted strikes as talks apparently restarted in hopes of some type of diplomatic solution. Trump called them "very friendly negotiations", though Tehran denied any discussions were happening. But following the Iranian missile attack on a US base in Jordan on Tuesday, Trump vowed to retaliate, telling reporters at the White House: "We're going to be hitting them very hard because it's our turn to hit them.  They know it's coming. They asked us not to do it."The latest wave of US strikes started at 20:00 ET on Wednesday (01:00 BST on Thursday) and lasted about an hour, with Centcom calling them a "powerful response to yesterday's attempted Iranian attacks on US forces based in the Middle East". All of Iran's missiles were intercepted, Centcom said. The attack by the US targeted "military command centers, missile and drone facilities, coastal surveillance and defense sites, and maritime capabilities," Centcom wrote once the strikes were complete.Iranian state media agency Irib reported that the islands of Qeshm and Abadan, both central to the oil industry, were among the areas hit.  "A US attack on a residential home in the Chah Tangu neighbourhood of Qeshm killed three members of a family: the father, the mother, and their 2-year-old child," Fars reported citing the Hormozgan University of Medical Sciences.A man in his 30s living in the south of the island told BBC Persian he was heading to Tehran, because "things are becoming more dangerous here"."Our internet situation has been a mess. The electricity has been cutting out several times since this morning," he said. "There have been loud bangs since 03:40 this morning. We are helpless."Meanwhile, Jordan's armed forces said that air defence systems had successfully shot down five Iranian missiles targeting the Kingdom's territory on Thursday.On Tuesday, the IRGC said it had targeted a US air base and a command centre in Jordan "in response to the acts of aggression of the American child-killing army".It also said naval forces had struck three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz after they "ignored warnings" and sailed along what it described as an "unsafe and illegal route" through the vital Gulf waterway.Last Friday, Trump suspended an intensive bombing campaign that had lasted for 13 consecutive nights. The US said it had targeted Iranian weapons and military sites. Scores of people were reported to have died.On Tuesday, Centcom said the joint US-Saudi strikes hit "multiple terrorist logistics and weapons sites across eastern Iraq in a strong response to over 30 IRGC-directed aerial drone attacks in the last 72 hours".Iraq's paramilitary Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), which is dominated by Iran-backed Shia militias, said at least 20 of its members had been killed in US-Saudi strikes on its bases.The Iraqi presidency said it denounced the bombing of the PMF bases, calling it "an unacceptable attack and a blatant violation of Iraq's sovereignty".But Trump told Fox News the strikes had been "co-ordinated with the Iraqi government".Saudi Arabia, which sees itself as the leading Sunni Muslim power, and Iran, the largest Shia Muslim country, have been locked in a struggle for regional dominance for decades.With additional reporting from Ghoncheh Habibiazad, BBC Persian

schema.headline: US launches 'heavy' strikes on Iran after attempted attack on American troops
